title: The Five Stages of AI Maturity in Engineering Organizations - Where and Why Teams Get Stuck
gist: Quotient CEO Lizzie Matusov argues that record enterprise AI spend ($2.5T projected in 2026, +47% YoY) is failing to convert into software delivery gains because every SDLC is rate-limited by a single bottleneck that more tokens cannot bypass. She lays out a five-stage AI maturity model built from ~15 research papers, researcher interviews and 100+ org interviews, and argues token-usage metrics are a more dangerous productivity proxy than lines of code because each token carries a literal dollar cost.

insights.claim: Global AI spending grew 47% year-over-year in 2026 to a projected $2.5 trillion, with 72% of enterprises now running at least one AI workload in production.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: Sets the denominator for the ROI question: at $2.5T, even modest evidence of productivity conversion becomes the key swing factor for AI infrastructure demand durability.
insights.quote: Just in 2026, we've seen a 47% year-over-year growth in global AI spending. We are now projected to spend $2.5 trillion on AI, and 72% of enterprises are running at least one AI workload in production.
insights.locator: I think one truth that all of us have felt

insights.claim: Uber burned through its entire 2026 AI budget in four months, and its CTO said the company could not find a stable relationship between AI expenditure and productivity output.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: A named, large-scale enterprise publicly failing to attribute ROI is the leading indicator to watch for AI budget discipline in 2027 planning cycles.
insights.quote: Curiously, when asked about the return, the CTO said that, frankly, they could not find a stable equivalent relationship between the expenditure and the productivity output.
insights.locator: Let's take Uber, for example

insights.claim: Microsoft announced it is dropping Claude Code by the end of the month because it blew past its budget, and its transcripts likewise do not articulate an ROI for the AI usage.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: Coding-agent vendors face budget-driven churn risk at the largest accounts; watch enterprise seat/consumption renewals rather than announced adoption.
insights.quote: Even more recently, Microsoft just announced that they're going to be dropping Claude Code by the end of this month due to the budget and the way that they blew right past it.
insights.locator: Even more recently, Microsoft just announced

insights.claim: The core puzzle of enterprise AI is that developers report clear individual efficiency gains while those gains do not aggregate into organizational outcomes.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: The individual-to-organizational conversion rate, not adoption rate, is the metric that determines whether AI spend is defensible in the next budget cycle.
insights.quote: Then, why is it that individual usage is not translating to organizational outcomes?
insights.locator: The thing is, we know we're getting value out of AI

insights.claim: Guidance about how much AI to consume should be discounted by the incentives of whoever issues it, as when the advice that a $500k engineer should consume $250k of tokens comes from a company that profits directly if the advice is followed.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: Vendor-sourced adoption benchmarks are marketing, not benchmarks; treat token-consumption targets from chip and model suppliers as demand-generation, and discount them when modeling sustainable enterprise spend.
insights.quote: if Jensen Huang is saying that he would be deeply alarmed if his $500k engineer didn't consume at least $250k of tokens, you might want to ask yourself, why is Jensen Huang giving that advice?
insights.locator: Oftentimes, I encourage people to think about the incentives

themes.theme: Theory of constraints applied to the SDLC

insights.claim: Every production system is limited by a single bottleneck, so maximizing throughput at every other station does not raise output and actively degrades the system.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: Provides the mechanism for why AI coding spend fails to show up in delivery metrics, and tells buyers where incremental spend should actually go.
insights.quote: Every system is limited by a single bottleneck. If you're trying to speed up everything else, it's not going to increase the output if you don't actually address that bottleneck.
insights.locator: This is the theory of constraints

insights.claim: Running every station at capacity produces three predictable failures: work-in-progress inventory explodes behind the bottleneck, lead times lengthen, and quality problems compound.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: These three symptoms are the observable tell that an org is over-invested in AI generation relative to its review and validation capacity.
insights.locator: Three things will happen

insights.claim: Increasing token spend or code volume produces no throughput gain when the constraint sits in code review, testing, or deployment gates rather than in code generation.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: Implies the next spend wave shifts from generation tools toward review, testing and deployment automation — the actual constraints.
insights.locator: Let's say that you have a bottleneck in the code review process

insights.claim: The 2025 DORA report, covering roughly 5,000 technology professionals, found individual effectiveness rose while software delivery throughput did not meaningfully change.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: Independent large-sample confirmation that the productivity story is not yet visible in delivery metrics — a warning for anyone underwriting AI-driven margin expansion.
insights.locator: Actually, the DORA report in 2025 also found this

insights.claim: Bottlenecks are org-specific and even team-specific, so there is no transferable playbook for where AI investment will pay off inside a given company.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: Undercuts one-size-fits-all AI rollout products and favors diagnostic/measurement tooling that locates the local constraint.
insights.locator: The thing is that bottlenecks can look different for every organization

insights.claim: The maturity model was constructed from a synthesis of about 15 research papers, interviews with the designers of DORA and SPACE, and field discovery across more than 100 organizations that named AI a top goal.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: Signals a research-methodology moat for the vendor and a rare non-vendor-incentivized benchmark buyers can use against supplier claims.
insights.locator: We first did a synthesis of about 15 different research papers

insights.claim: AI productivity research older than roughly six months should be treated as outdated because of the capability inflection point at the start of 2026.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: Any diligence or thesis built on 2025 developer-productivity studies has a short shelf life; re-underwrite frequently.
insights.quote: We also were careful not to go back too far. Anything more than six months feels a little bit outdated, especially with the inflection point that came at the beginning of this year.
insights.locator: We looked at papers focused on AI's impact

insights.claim: Each of the five maturity stages is scored across six characteristics: enablement, policy and governance, validation and testing, embedding in workflows, workflow automation, and data context and access.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: A concrete scorecard for diligence on how deeply a target company has actually operationalized AI versus merely purchased seats.
insights.locator: Each of those five stages is defined by six characteristics

insights.claim: Stage two, assisted development, reliably produces a bifurcation between early adopters who push through imperfect output and skeptics who abandon the tools after two or three attempts.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: Explains why seat-based adoption metrics overstate real usage — the skeptic cohort inflates licenses without generating value.
insights.locator: We also see the bifurcation of usage start to happen in stage two

insights.claim: The defining failure of stage two is that the harnesses and systems surrounding code have not been adjusted for the increased volume AI generates across the SDLC.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: Points directly at where the unmet spend sits: test infrastructure, review automation and CI capacity, not more model licenses.
insights.locator: I think what's important about stage two

insights.claim: The jump from stage two to stage three is the largest and most capital-intensive because it requires building development harnesses — automated validation of AI-generated code, embedded AI in linting and review, and auto-triggered workflows.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific tooling category — validation and review infrastructure — most likely to see budget as orgs cross stage two to three.
insights.quote: There's a pretty big jump from stage two to stage three, because this is where we're starting to focus on the development harnesses around our code.
insights.locator: Stage three is what we would call standardized workflows

insights.claim: Agents only enter the model at stage four, and the infrastructure built in stages one through three is the precondition for safely handing them control.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: Contradicts the market narrative that agents are a drop-in purchase; agent-platform revenue is gated by prior investment in testing and governance.
insights.quote: I am many minutes into my talk, and I did not say the word agent once. That is because it is really important to think about the infrastructure from stages one to three
insights.locator: I am many minutes into my talk

insights.claim: Stage four is characterized by agents executing bounded low-complexity tasks with a human approving, such as an agent picking up a P3 support ticket and generating a PR that a person reviews and deploys.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: A usable definition of what production agent deployment actually looks like today — useful for filtering vendor claims of autonomy.
insights.locator: A great example of a stage four automation

insights.claim: The operational test for stage five is whether agents have been given the exact same ownership and autonomy an organization would grant a senior engineer, including merging and handling production incidents.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: A crisp benchmark to test 'AI-native' marketing claims; almost no enterprise passes it today.
insights.quote: When you've given agents the exact amount of ownership and autonomy you'd give to a senior engineer, that's when you've really hit stage five.
insights.locator: The way that we describe that feeling of stage five

insights.claim: Stage five requires a structured organizational knowledge graph so agents can access anything an engineer could, making internal data infrastructure the gating asset for full autonomy.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: Full-autonomy narratives depend on an internal-data-infrastructure buildout most enterprises have not started — a durable demand driver and a timing check on agent adoption.
insights.locator: In order for it to have the same amount of ownership

themes.theme: Where organizations actually sit, and the risk curve

insights.claim: Across dozens of companies studied, the average large enterprise sits between stage two and three while the average growth-stage company sits between stage three and four, driven by enterprises' higher complexity, headcount and regulatory load such as public listing or FedRAMP.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: Calibrates realistic enterprise AI penetration far below headline narratives; enterprise agent revenue is likely 1-2 stages away, not imminent.
insights.quote: In our work with dozens of companies, we actually found that the average big enterprise is somewhere between stage two and three. The average growth stage organization is somewhere between stage three and four.
insights.locator: What is the right stage for your org?

insights.claim: Risk is not monotonic in AI maturity: stage one carries shadow-IT and competitive-innovation risk, while stage five carries the risk that agents operating faster than humans can review will erode software quality and customer trust.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: Reframes maximal autonomy as a risk position, not a goal — relevant for anyone underwriting companies claiming full agentic deployment.
insights.quote: That's because the risk is not monotonic in maturity.
insights.locator: What's interesting is that we don't often find people at the polar opposite poles

insights.claim: The recommended 2026 target for most organizations is stages three to four, not stage five, despite headlines implying every org will reach end-to-end autonomy within two months.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: A concrete near-term ceiling on realistic enterprise agent adoption to test against vendor forecasts.
insights.locator: That's why for most organizations we recommend targeting

insights.claim: The correct diagnostic sequence is to score each of the six capabilities independently, invest in the one or two weakest, then identify the next-stage unlock — because gaps between capability levels are exactly where bottlenecks form.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: Actionable diagnostic: uneven capability profiles, not low average maturity, predict where delivery stalls.
insights.locator: There are three steps to diagnose your stage

insights.claim: An organization's AI maturity reflects the average team, which typically lags the maturity of its most advanced teams, so leadership self-assessments based on leading teams systematically overstate readiness.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: Explains the persistent gap between executive AI claims and delivered outcomes — diligence should sample the median team, not the showcase one.
insights.locator: Your organization's AI maturity is representative of how an average team would respond

themes.theme: Why token metrics are actively harmful

insights.claim: Token usage as a productivity proxy is more dangerous than lines of code, because lines of code carried only indirect costs through complexity and technical debt while every token has a literal dollar value attached the moment the behavior is incentivized.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: Implies token-based internal incentives directly inflate cloud and model spend without output — a margin risk hiding inside AI budgets.
insights.quote: I would argue that token maxing or using tokens as a proxy for AI's impact on productivity is a much more dangerous measure than lines of code.
insights.locator: Measuring Outcomes, Not Usage

insights.claim: A Concordia University study of token usage across 30 agent-run development tasks found code reviews consumed about 60% of tokens, driven by back-and-forth between developers and agents.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: Quantifies where agent inference spend actually lands — review iteration, not generation — reframing which part of the workflow drives model revenue.
insights.locator: recent study at Concordia University looked at token usage

insights.claim: Tokens in agentic development are disproportionately spent on input rather than output or reasoning, a communication tax paid to convey context rather than to produce work.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: Input-heavy token mix favors providers with cheap long-context and caching economics, and makes context infrastructure a cost lever rather than a feature.
insights.quote: Researchers again pointed to the communication tax where a lot of our tokens are actually spent on communicating context rather than generating output.
insights.locator: Then, tokens were disproportionately spent on input

insights.claim: Token leaderboards trigger Goodhart's law in practice: a senior engineer at a well-known FAANG company described deliberately inflating token metrics by asking AI questions already answered in documentation, prototyping features he intends to discard, and defaulting to agents on tasks he could do faster by hand.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: Direct evidence that a measurable share of enterprise token consumption is metric-gaming, not demand — a quality-of-revenue question for inference providers.
insights.quote: I am conscious of not wanting to be seen as 'uses too little AI.' I'm not ashamed to say that I do token maxing here.
insights.locator: In a recent Substack called the Pragmatic Engineer

insights.claim: Amazon shut down its internal token leaderboard, with a senior VP writing in an internal memo that employees should not use AI for the sake of using AI.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: First visible large-cap retreat from usage-maximizing incentives; if it spreads, artificially inflated enterprise token demand deflates.
insights.quote: Please don't use AI just for the sake of using AI. Use it to help you solve customer problems, to help you solve business problems.
insights.locator: In fact, so much so that over the weekend, Amazon shut down its token leaderboard

insights.claim: The industry measures tokens for the same reason it once measured lines of code — the streetlight effect, searching where measurement is easy rather than where the truth lies.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: A durable mental model for discounting any AI adoption statistic that is easy to collect and disconnected from delivered outcomes.
insights.quote: We search for answers where it's easy to find, not necessarily where we know the truth lies.
insights.locator: This is the streetlight effect

themes.theme: Outcome frameworks that replace usage metrics

insights.claim: Google's research team measures productivity through speed, quality and ease — getting value to customers fast, maintaining excellence to retain trust, and keeping development friction-free and predictable — deliberately holding those three in tension to resist single-metric gaming.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: A lightweight, tension-based scorecard that is harder to game than token or seat counts when assessing whether AI is actually working.
insights.locator: The first one is very simple: speed, quality, ease

insights.claim: SPACE, built by Nicole Forsgren and the Microsoft Research team around satisfaction and well-being, performance, activity, communication and collaboration, and efficiency and flow, targets team friction and outcomes, whereas DORA focuses on software stability.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: Clarifies which measurement framework surfaces AI bottlenecks versus which measures stability — they answer different questions.
insights.locator: The other one, which I'm sure some of you have heard of before, is the SPACE framework

insights.claim: At a recent researcher summit, the original SPACE authors reaffirmed the 2021 framework, concluding that a holistic, outcomes-based, tension-oriented approach remains the best way to understand AI's impact despite the framework predating the AI boom.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: Suggests no new AI-native productivity metric has earned researcher consensus — treat vendor-proposed AI productivity indices skeptically.
insights.locator: Recently, the researchers came together for a summit

insights.claim: Rising AI usage alongside flat delivery outcomes is a diagnostic signal that a new bottleneck has formed, and resolving one bottleneck predictably exposes the next one elsewhere in the system.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: The usage-versus-outcome divergence is a monitorable leading indicator; treat it as a trigger to reallocate AI budget rather than to increase it.
insights.quote: when usage grows but delivery outcomes aren't improving, this is what can signal new bottlenecks are happening.
insights.locator: To tie things back

insights.claim: As the cost of tokens and of leveraging AI rises, outcome measurement shifts from a nice-to-have to a budget-defense necessity for engineering leaders.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: Implies rising inference prices, not falling ones, and a growing market for engineering-outcome measurement tooling.
insights.quote: Especially as the cost of tokens and the cost of leveraging AI goes up, it becomes really important to understand what is the outcome of all of that work.
insights.locator: Actionable Takeaways

insights.claim: The two behaviors that separate effective engineering organizations are thoughtfully improving AI usage across the whole SDLC and resolving the bottlenecks that limit outcomes — stated as the talk's single repeated thesis.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: A two-question screen for whether a company's AI investment will convert to delivered results.
insights.quote: Again, the most effective organizations do two things. One, they thoughtfully improve AI usage across the software development life cycle. Two, they resolve the bottlenecks that limit their outcomes.
insights.locator: Number four, watch the gap

insights.claim: Research in developer productivity is turning over fast enough that a paper published three months from now can negate a finding read two weeks ago.
insights.speaker: Lizzie Matusov
insights.so_what: Argues for continuous re-underwriting of AI productivity assumptions rather than annual review cycles.
insights.quote: I will tell you sometimes a paper from three months from now will negate something we read about two weeks ago.
insights.locator: Resources
